migrate

/MY-grayt/ - the stress falls on MY · verb

Hear It

What It Means

Migrate means to move from one region to another, usually with the seasons.

Hawk-watch volunteers on the ridge count broadwings by the kettle-full as the birds migrate south on the September thermals.

Example

Band number CE93715 belongs to an Arctic tern, and the arithmetic on her file reads like a misprint. Every year of her life she has migrated from the top of the world to the bottom and back — Greenland to the Antarctic pack ice — chasing an endless polar summer. She is over twenty years old. The biologists who tallied her lifetime distance stopped comparing it to other birds and started comparing it to the moon.

Migrate is the exact word for what she does, because it means to move from one region to another, usually with the seasons — and, crucially, to come back. The tern is not lost and not emigrating; her twice-yearly journey is a round trip written into the species itself, the same route renewed every year of her long life.

Compare the words

Synonyms · words with a similar meaning

journey: To journey is simply to make a long trip — any direction, any season, one-way or round. To migrate is narrower: a whole population moves between regions on the calendar, usually meaning to come back. Every migration is a journey; almost no journey is a migration.

trek: A trek is one long, hard push overland — a single grueling passage with a start, an end, and blisters in between. To migrate is to repeat a route: out with one season, back with another, year upon year.

What it isn’t · antonyms and near-opposites

remain: to stay where you are as the seasons turn

hibernate: to sit the hard season out in one den instead of outrunning it

Where it sits · how fixed and final the destination is

roam → migrate → resettle

roam vs. migrate: To roam is to drift wherever the grass looks better today, with no destination at all — a looser wandering than migrate, whose route runs to a fixed region and back.

resettle vs. migrate: Resettle goes past migrate — the migrating animal means to come back with the season; to resettle is to move once, put down roots, and stay for good.

Build the Word

The pieces

Root — migr-: to move from one home to another (Latin migrare)

Suffix — -ate: to do, to act

Put it together: Migr- (to move one's home) + -ate (to do) = to make the move. Latin migrare was about changing where you live, not merely where you stand — and every English relative keeps that sense of home in motion: migrants, migration, and the immigrant who has moved in.

Use the root in a new word: immigrant: An immigrant is migr- wearing the prefix im- (in): one who has moved in, into a new country to live.

Root Check

Word Choice

neutral / scientific

Migrate is the biologist's and demographer's word for populations moving between regions — usually tied to the seasons, usually a round trip. Keep it apart from two unit-mates: the itinerant worker travels a circuit for work in any season, and animals forage once they arrive — the moving and the meal-hunting are different verbs. Files and software migrate too, a borrowed sense; keys and coffee mugs just get moved.
